sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: What does the home and school language divide indicate?
questions.answer: A situation where the medium of instruction at school is different from the language used at home.

questions.q: According to NCF 2005, how should India's linguistic diversity be seen?
questions.answer: As a resource to promote multilingual proficiency in a child.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Indian Constitution aims to protect the ________ nature of India.
questions.answer: multilingual

questions.q: Which languages should be valued equally?
questions.answer: All languages, including tribal languages as well as English.

questions.q: How does NCF 2005 propose to handle first-generation learners?
questions.answer: Teach them in the mother tongue in the initial years, with less stress on a second and third language.

questions.q: Why is less stress put on a second and third language for first-generation learners?
questions.answer: Because support to learn these languages may not be available to the child at home.

sections.passage: India is a multilingual country, and its Constitution is committed to protecting the multilingual nature of India. The home and school language divide indicates the situation where the medium of instruction at school is different from the language used at home. NCF, 2005 respects the multilingual character of Indian society and suggests it should be seen as a resource to promote multilingual proficiency in a child. All languages, including tribal languages as well as English, should be valued equally. All mother tongues are appreciated as an important link between the young child and the school. In the case of a first-generation learner, teaching in the initial years should be in the mother tongue, with less stress on learning a second and third language, as support may not be available to the child at home to learn these languages. (October 2024)

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks or one-word answers).

questions.q: State True or False: (i) Diversity gives recognition, acceptance and respect to individual differences irrespective of their origin. (ii) Mother tongue is the language spoken at home.
questions.answer: (i) True. (ii) True.

questions.q: State True or False: (i) Children should be discouraged from sharing their religious beliefs with their peers. (ii) An auditory learner enjoys listening to stories.
questions.answer: (i) False — they should be encouraged to recognise and appreciate differences. (ii) True.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks (choose the correct word): (i) Using the mother tongue in preschool and primary school leads to fewer ________ (retention/dropouts). (ii) The medium of instruction is the language used at ________ (home/school).
questions.answer: (i) dropouts (ii) school

questions.q: Match: (a) Caste (b) Ethnicity — (i) Belonging to a social group with common regional and cultural traditions (ii) A system of classification determined by birth (iii) Division of humankind by physical features
Answer in one sentence: (i) What is race? (ii) What is gender?
questions.answer: (i) Race is the division of humankind on the basis of physical features such as height and skin and eye colour, and social behaviour. (ii) Gender is the social and cultural identity associated with being a boy or a girl.
questions.note: April 2023 asked for a one-sentence explanation of race.

questions.q: Answer in one word or phrase: (i) The use of more than one language by a person or community. (ii) What should a teacher choose a toy for — the child's sex or the skill it develops?
questions.answer: (i) Multilingualism (ii) The skill it develops

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Discuss the implications of socio-economic status in learning.
questions.answer: Children of low and high socio-economic groups differ in clothes, school bags and stationery, which shows clearly where there is no uniform. All children must be treated equally and given space in textbooks, curriculum and activities; uniforms reflect this. Each child's different experiences can be used as a teaching-learning resource.

or.q: Define diversity with the help of an example.
or.answer: Diversity means uniqueness or differences among people — in culture, religion, language, ability, socio-economic status, learning style — without any judgment attached; it gives recognition and respect to individual differences. Example: in a class, children share the special foods their families cook for different festivals.

questions.q: What is multilingualism?
questions.answer: Using, or promoting the use of, several languages by an individual or a community. In India each region has its own language and dialect; children of different languages study together, so teachers should respect the home language and build on it. Sign language and Braille are also to be valued.

questions.q: Describe any two steps an ECCE teacher could take to minimise the effects of the home-school language divide.
questions.answer: Any two: use the mother tongue as the medium in the early years and gradually introduce the second and third language; respect and accept the home language and build on its strengths; use local stories, songs, riddles and art; learn common words of the children's languages; involve parents.

questions.q: How can children with physical disabilities be involved in classroom activities?
questions.answer: By small changes in pedagogy: sign language during rhyme time for a child with hearing impairment; colouring sheets with tactile outlines (thread, sticks, a bangle for a circle) for a child with visual impairment; learning home signs from parents and using flash cards; consulting a sign-language expert or special educator.

questions.q: How can an ECCE teacher promote equitable participation of all children through telling stories?
questions.answer: By choosing stories carefully and noticing how boys and girls are shown (are fairies always girls, are women always in the kitchen?), then discussing role reversals — a story where the mother goes to the office and the father cooks — so that stereotypes are questioned.

questions.q: What is caste? How can schools avoid caste discrimination?
questions.answer: Caste is a system of rigid social categories decided by birth, with hereditary status and social barriers. Schools must treat all children equally and avoid discrimination in serving mid-day meals, seating arrangements and involving children in learning activities.
questions.note: October 2022 asked for a one-sentence explanation of caste.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: What steps will you take to ensure gender-equitable participation of children in a preschool?
questions.answer: Choose toys and materials for the skills they develop, not by the child's sex, and prefer gender-neutral toys such as puzzles, blocks and clay; choose stories carefully and discuss role reversals; encourage fair play — all toys within reach of all and structured time for every child with the kitchen set, ball and swings, outdoor games for all; encourage friendships and mixed teams; avoid gender-based work distribution and invite both boys and girls to help with food or tidying.

or.q: What are the implications of multilingualism for an ECCE centre?
or.answer: Children of different home languages study together; if instruction is only in another language they struggle, lose confidence and may drop out. So the centre should respect and use the home language, build the second and third language on its strengths, use local stories, songs and riddles, value sign language and Braille, and see multilingualism as a resource (NCF 2005).

questions.q: Why is it important to address diversity within the school environment?
questions.answer: Children come from different races, castes, languages, religions, ethnic groups, genders, socio-economic backgrounds, abilities and learning styles. Addressing diversity makes every child feel accepted and safe, prevents stereotypes and discrimination, uses children's varied experiences as a resource for mutual learning and celebration, and has academic and socio-emotional benefits.

or.q: How can a teacher demonstrate an understanding of diversity in the classroom?
or.answer: By linking lessons to children's lives (festival food sharing), holding food, dress and story days, using the home language, choosing roles and stories without stereotypes, adapting activities for children with disabilities, using several teaching methods for different learning styles, and treating all children equally irrespective of caste, gender or status.

questions.q: How do diverse groups in a school environment provide opportunities for mutual learning?
questions.answer: Each child brings experiences of different customs, festivals, food, languages and ways of life. Sharing these — food days, festival discussions, stories and songs in different languages — lets children learn from one another, explore and celebrate in a safe, nurturing environment, appreciate differences, develop respect and empathy, and learn that all are equal.

questions.q: What are the effects of the home and school language divide on children?
questions.answer: Children cannot make friends easily, cannot read, write and express themselves, and perform poorly; repeated failure lowers self-esteem and confidence and raises dropout; they feel no belonging to school; they are less likely to enrol and succeed; parents participate less; and children lose pride in their identity and heritage.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What do you understand by the term 'diversity'? What are the main factors leading to diversity?
questions.answer: Diversity (from the Latin 'diversus') means differences — the unique characteristics of people, visible and invisible, without any judgment; it gives recognition, acceptance and respect to individual differences. Factors: race (physical features — avoid stereotypes such as fair children as fairies); caste (status by birth — avoid discrimination in meals and seating); multilingualism (different home languages — respect the mother tongue, value sign language and Braille); ethnicity (regional and cultural traditions — festival, food and dress days); gender (social identity of boys and girls — equal participation, separate toilets); socio-economic status (treat all equally, uniforms); physical disability (adapt activities); religious beliefs (appreciate festivals, promote secularism); age; level of physical activity; and cognitive or learning style (teach in several ways).
questions.note: October 2021 asked for a one-sentence explanation of diversity.

questions.q: What are stereotypes? Explain the influence of gender and caste stereotypes on children and how a teacher can avoid them.
questions.answer: Stereotypes are fixed ideas or assumptions about a group of people based on traits like race, sex, caste or religion, which may not be true of every member. They ignore individual abilities, are prejudicial, limit choices and lead to discrimination. Gender stereotypes expect boys to be strong, logical, brave decision makers and girls to be dependent, emotional housekeepers; media strengthen them, and children then limit their play, interests and ambitions. Caste stereotypes lower the self-worth of children of so-called lower castes and lead to discrimination in seating and meals. Teachers should treat all children alike, choose toys by skill, use stories with role reversal, form mixed teams, share work equally, avoid labels and comments based on caste or appearance, and model respect for all.
